set.statement: In people who use drugs in North America who tested their drugs (or, in one study, their urine) with fentanyl test strips, on their own without supervision or with staff at a supervised injection site (2016 to 2023), a result showing fentanyl was followed, by people's own account or by intentions they stated to staff, by a safer way of using in a minority to a majority of cases, most often using less or going slower, and seldom by throwing the drug away; no study read observed what people then took. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017), of 31 young adults who said a strip had shown fentanyl, 45 in 100 said they then used smaller amounts, 42 went slower, 39 used with someone else around, 36 tried a small amount first (a 'tester'), 10 threw the drugs out, 10 sold them and 7 gave them away; these answers were given at least two weeks later, the results were not checked, and how many used the drugs as usual was not reported. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), staff recorded an intention to use less after 142 of 391 checks before use that showed fentanyl (36 in 100), against 7 of 122 that did not (6 in 100), and an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 (11 in 100) against 10 of 134 (7 in 100); what people then did was not recorded. In a British Columbia take-home programme (2019), asked a standard question (not about their own results) about what they did when a strip showed fentanyl, 217 of 336 answers (65 in 100) described no change, 86 (26 in 100) at least one safer change and 6 (2 in 100) a riskier one (using alone, or using more or faster). Reviews relay a median of 55 in 100 (23 to 75 in 100, seven studies) reporting some safer change, and people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl; the evidence is mostly intentions or self-reports (one review counts 22 of its 31 behaviour studies as measuring intentions), with no comparison of people given strips with people not given them; both reviews include the Rhode Island and Vancouver studies. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: When a strip showed fentanyl, some people said they used less, went slower, used with someone else nearby or tried a small amount first. Few said they threw the drug away, and in one programme about 2 in 3 answers described no change. All of this is what people said or planned: no study watched what they actually did, and no study compared people given strips with people not given them.
set.population: People who use drugs who tested their drugs (or, in one study, urine) with fentanyl test strips in North America, unsupervised or with staff: 31 young adults with a self-reported positive result in a Rhode Island pilot (2017); checks before use at a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016–17); 336 survey answers from 218 people in a British Columbia take-home programme (2019); studies relayed by a scoping review (to March 2023) and a systematic review (to October 2019)
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Intentions and standard-question answers stand in for what people did; all North American settings where fentanyl was common; among the studies read, responses to a negative result were reported only at the Vancouver site, and only as intentions.

evidence_set: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Data collection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: the lead sentence now says 'by people's own account or by intentions they stated to staff' (the Vancouver figures are staff-recorded intentions; second reader 147) and 'on their own without supervision' instead of 'at home' (the Rhode Island pilot does not say where people tested, and take-home strips in British Columbia were used at home, in the street and at supervised sites; second readers 145 and 144); 'mostly intentions' is now attributed to the review that counts them (22 of its 31 behaviour studies; the scoping review files most changes as actual behaviour; second reader 144), and 'without a comparison group' became 'no comparison of people given strips with people not given them' (some relayed studies compare positive with negative results or with people who used no strip); the indirectness note no longer says that responses to a negative result are not reported, which the claim's own Vancouver figures contradict; plain text and population aligned; the Vancouver anchor's locator adds Methods › Data collection, where staff recording is described (targeted check note, reader 147). No rating or status changed.

set.statement: In people who had drugs tested at an English festival (2016) or with fentanyl test strips in North America (2016 to 2019), a result showing that a drug was not what it had been sold as, or that it contained fentanyl, compared with a result that did not, is associated with more people getting rid of drugs, but how many depended greatly on the setting: two thirds at the festival when the drug proved not as sold, about one in ten or fewer after a strip showed fentanyl. At one English festival, where chemists tested drugs on site and staff gave each result in a consultation, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not what it had been sold as (67 in 100) handed over drugs for police destruction, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched (9 in 100); the service saw these handovers, but people may have kept or thrown away other drugs elsewhere, and 111 of the 164 with a matching result said they would take their usual amount. After a strip showed fentanyl, few people said they would get rid of the drug, or had done so: at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 checks before use that showed fentanyl (11 in 100), against 10 of 134 that did not (7 in 100), a difference that may be chance (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.79 to 3.26), and in a Rhode Island pilot 10 in 100 of 31 young adults with a positive strip said they threw the drugs out. A systematic review of drug checking services to 2019 counts eight studies with disposal as an outcome and prints rates for four of them (editors' count), from 0 to 10 in 100 (observed at Canadian festivals at 4 and 7 in 100); it reports more disposal after unexpected results and counts this English festival among the eight without giving its rate, while an earlier evidence brief cited by the festival study gives 4 to 76 in 100 across evaluations. The authors of the Vancouver study suggest that the low rate there may reflect dependence, lack of money to replace drugs and no access to unadulterated drugs. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: At one festival where chemists tested drugs, 67 in 100 people whose drug was not what it had been sold as handed over drugs to be destroyed, against 9 in 100 whose drug matched. After a strip showed fentanyl, few people said they would throw the drug away, or had done so: about 10 in 100. Most of these figures are what people said; only the festival handovers were seen by staff.
set.magnitude: Festival (observed): 30/45 (66.7%; Wilson 52.1–78.6%) against 15/164 (9.1%; 5.6–14.5%), p < .01; difference 57.5 points (Newcombe 42.0–70.0), risk ratio 7.3 (editors' calculations); 49/230 (21.3%) overall; stated intention to take the usual amount 111/164 (67.7%) with a matching result against 4/45 (8.9%) with a non-matching one. Vancouver (stated, before use): 50/436 (11.5%) against 10/134 (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26); risk difference 4.0 points (−2.3 to 8.7, editors' calculation). Rhode Island (self-report, n = 31): threw out 10%, sold 10%, gave away 7%. Review (relayed): rates printed for 4 of its 8 studies with disposal as an outcome (editors' count), 0–10%; observed 4% (n = 2078) and 7% (n = 2786) at Canadian festivals; no rate printed for the English festival, which it counts among the eight. Evidence brief cited by the festival study: 4–76% across evaluations.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The size differs greatly (67 in 100 at the festival after a drug proved not as sold, about 10 in 100 after a positive strip), in line with the setting: festival-goers whose drug was not as sold, against people at a supervised injection site and young adults in a pilot, for whom fentanyl was common and often expected; the direction is the same.
set.grade.domains.large_effect.note: Not applied: the festival risk ratio of 7.3 is unadjusted and comes from self-selected clients, many already worried about their sample, so the condition of METHODS §6.3 (an effect that stays large under adjustment, with no remaining bias away from the null) is not met.

evidence_set: Before use, a stated intention to dispose of the drug followed 50 of 436 fentanyl-positive checks (11.5%) and 10 of 134 negative checks (7.5%), OR 1.60 (95% CI 0.79–3.26). The authors suggest that the low rate may reflect dependence on the drugs, lack of money to replace them and no access to unadulterated drugs, and contrast a 2015 festival service where 13% disposed of drugs after an unexpected result and 2% after an expected one. Editors' calculation (card): risk difference 4.0 percentage points (Newcombe 95% CI −2.3 to 8.7).
change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: the lead sentence names the two kinds of result (a drug not as sold; fentanyl on a strip) instead of 'something unexpected', and drops 'though most did not', which does not hold for the festival's not-as-sold group (two thirds handed drugs over; second reader 145); the strip sentence no longer says 'people who use opioids' and says that few said they would get rid of the drug or had done so (Vancouver recorded intentions; checks were of client-reported substances, and the Rhode Island sample was not limited to opioids; second readers 147 and 145); the review's 0 to 10 in 100 is now given as the rates it prints for four of its eight disposal studies, with the festival counted among the eight without a rate (second reader 147, targeted check 147), and the 4 to 76 in 100 of an earlier evidence brief cited by the festival study is added from an existing anchor (second reader 145); 'link' became 'suggest' for the Vancouver authors' reasons, here and in that anchor (targeted check note, reader 147: the source hedges them); the large-effect domain now says why the festival risk ratio of 7.3 is not upgraded; inconsistency note and plain text aligned. No rating or status changed.

set.statement: In people who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America, using fentanyl test strips compared with not using them: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of overdose. The only study read that compared the two groups followed 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio for four weeks in 2023: after allowing for state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and the drugs used each day, and also for strip use and risk-reduction behaviours reported during the four weeks, which may carry part of any difference strips make, the modelled risk of a self-reported overdose that people survived (passing out and needing to be revived) was about 2 in 100 days of drug use in both groups (0.02 a day; risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06, compatible with 30% fewer overdoses or twice as many); before that adjustment it was twice as high in the people who used strips (risk ratio 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89), who more often injected and used fentanyl; deaths could not be counted. A scoping review of 91 studies to March 2023 found only two that reported overdose outcomes, neither comparing people who tested with people who did not: at a supervised injection site most checks came after use (113 of the 120 overdoses were recorded with checks made after use, and a check may have been prompted by the overdose), so its lower odds of overdose among people who said they would use less (crude odds ratio 0.41) cannot show an effect; and after a vending machine began giving out strips with naloxone, county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%, with no control area. A systematic review of drug checking to 2019 found no other study linking testing with overdose. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In the one study that compared people who used test strips with people who did not, over four weeks, overdoses that people survived were about as common in both groups once other differences were allowed for, but the result is too uncertain to rule out either fewer or more overdoses. That comparison also allowed for the safety steps people took during the study, which could hide a difference. Deaths could not be counted. No study read could show whether strips prevent overdoses or deaths.
set.magnitude: Vickers-Smith 2025: mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), from a model that also included the number of times strips were used and the risk-reduction score during follow-up (Table 3, note g); unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710); the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02). Karamouzian 2018 (card): 113 of 120 overdoses recorded with checks made after use; crude OR 0.41 (0.18–0.89) for intended dose reduction pools checks made before and after use and is not an effect. Kutscher 2024 (relayed): 2 of 91 studies with overdose outcomes; after a vending machine (10,155 strips with naloxone in its first year), county overdose deaths fell about 10% while Ohio's rose about 5%, with no control group.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Cohort: ROBINS-I serious (people chose to use strips; confounding by risk, with the crude ratio of 2.06 falling to 1.20 after an adjustment that left out injecting and earlier overdose but included strip use and risk-reduction behaviours during follow-up, which may hide part of any effect; 37 in 100 of those enrolled not analysed; self-reported outcomes). The two studies relayed by the review: no comparison of people who tested with people who did not, and checks that often followed the overdose.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness take one level each and imprecision two: very low. 'No detectable effect' would need an interval that excludes meaningful effects (METHODS §6.3), which this one does not, and the adjustment for behaviours during follow-up may also pull the estimate towards no difference, so the claim says the evidence is insufficient. Karamouzian et al.'s odds ratio of 0.41 is reported only to say why it cannot be read as an effect (card sc_karamouzian_2018, reporting issues); Karamouzian et al. is inside both reviews and is counted once. Status single study: only one study compared people who used strips with people who did not.

As read in the PubMed Central copy, note g lists for the overdose model: baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, and, for each drug-use day, the drug category, study week, part of the week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injecting, past 30-day overdose, ever having received strip instructions, education and employment are not in it (past overdose and strip instructions are in the behaviour models, note d; injecting is in neither). Editors' reading: the follow-up score and strip-use count come after the exposure and may carry part of any effect, which could pull the adjusted ratio towards 1.

change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: the list of what the overdose estimate was adjusted for is corrected: the Table 3 note for that model (g, read by second reader 147 in the PubMed Central copy) has state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, daily drug category and, during follow-up, strip use and the risk-reduction score, but not injecting or earlier overdose, which the claim had listed; the claim now says that the follow-up variables may carry part of any difference (new anchor, ai-located until a second reader checks it at the stated place); '113 of the 120 overdoses ... followed checks made after use' became 'were recorded with', since the order was not captured and a check may have been prompted by the overdose (second reader 147); 'neither with a comparison group' became 'neither comparing people who tested with people who did not' (the Vancouver study compares checks; second readers 147 and 144); risk-of-bias note, reasoning, magnitude and plain text aligned; the Maghsoudi anchor's locator adds where its 90 studies and October 2019 search are given (targeted check note, reader 147). No rating or status flag changed.

set.statement: In the 50 US states and the District of Columbia from 2018 to 2022, a state law making fentanyl test strips legal (16 jurisdictions with a dated law, from June 2018 to August 2022), compared with the same states before their law and with states that had no such law at the time, is associated with fewer deaths from drug overdose than the comparison predicted, in one state-level study (Bhai et al., 2025; no funding, no conflicts declared): about 7% fewer per 100,000 residents (6.7%, 95% CI 1.4% to 11.7%, without adjustment; 7.1%, 3.4% to 10.7%, adjusted for age, rurality and income; editors' calculation from the reported coefficients), which at the death rate in state-months with a law is roughly 2.6 to 2.8 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents a year (editors' rough calculation). With adjustment the figures were similar for White (8.0%) and Black residents (8.4%), though for Black residents the event studies show death rates above the comparison in every pre-law month they cover (editors' reading of the figures); the abstract's 13.5% for Black residents is the unadjusted estimate (11.9%) converted with its sign reversed. Unintentional overdose deaths, set against overdose deaths by suicide, homicide or undetermined intent, were 5% to 8% lower, with weak support without adjustment and no difference for Black residents with adjustment (−0.2%; 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%). This is a study of laws in whole state populations, not of people who used strips: it can show that death rates in these states ran below the comparison after their laws, but not that the laws or the strips caused it, nor whether people who tested their drugs were less likely to die. It did not measure whether strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug rather than opioid or fentanyl deaths, and it did not allow for other state policies or for changes in each state's drug supply at the same time; the fall appears from the first month of a law, which is hard to explain by strips that first had to be handed out and used (editors' reading), and the models used 2,613 of a possible 3,060 state-months without saying which were left out (editors' calculation). A 2026 correction says the authors modified some of the legal dates taken from their source and documented this in an online appendix not read here, and six states that the paper's map shows as legal have no date in its table, with no statement of how they were coded. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In one study of US states from 2018 to 2022, after a state made fentanyl test strips legal, drug deaths ran below what the trends in other states predicted: roughly 3 fewer deaths a year for every 100,000 people, or about 7 fewer for every 100 drug deaths expected. Results were about the same for White and Black residents once age, rural living and income were allowed for, though the result for Black residents is less certain. The study looked at laws and death records, not at people using strips. It did not check whether more strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug, and other changes at the same time could explain the difference. A later correction says the authors changed some of the law dates from their source.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious on the card (sc_bhai_2025): no adjustment for other state policies, federal strip funding from 2021 or changes in each state's drug supply; laws were adopted where death rates were higher; the event-study pre-period intervals are wide, and for Black residents every pre-period point lies above zero, with several 95% bands wholly above it (editors' reading of Figures 3 and 4); the fall appears from the month of the law; the exposure dates are the authors' modifications, documented only in an appendix not read, and six jurisdictions shaded legal on the map have no date; outcome codes are not given; 2,613 of a possible 3,060 state-months are used without explanation (1,469 for Black residents).

change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: added, from the anchors and the second reader's points (reader 145: supported, no overstatement): that for Black residents the event studies show death rates above the comparison before the laws (several pre-period bands lie wholly above zero in Figures 3 and 4, checked by the adjudicator on the rendered pages), that the fall appears from the first month of a law, that the models used 2,613 of a possible 3,060 state-months (editors' calculation, 51 jurisdictions × 60 months), and that the paper does not say how the six undated map states were coded; the plain text gives the absolute figure first and says the Black result is less certain; risk-of-bias note updated. No rating or status changed.

set.statement: In people who use drugs in North America who were offered fentanyl test strips, or who attended services that hand them out (studies from 2016 to 2023), how many used them varied widely with the setting and with what was counted. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017) that gave 93 young adults ten strips each, with training and naloxone, and paid them to come back, 62 of the 81 analysed (83 returned at least two weeks later) said they had used at least one (77 in 100; 62 of all 93, or 67 in 100, editors' calculation), a median of 3 strips, and 10 had used all ten; 58 in 100 had given strips to others. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), where staff offered a check to every client, about 1 in 100 visits included one (1,411 of 134,176 visits, by an unknown number of people). At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 of 732 clients (57 in 100) said they had used strips in the past 30 days. A scoping review of 91 studies to March 2023 relays documented use from 1 to 80 in 100 (median 19), against stated willingness of 43 to 85 in 100; it includes the Rhode Island pilot. A British Columbia take-home programme did not report how many kits it handed out, so its rate of use is unknown. Use was self-reported or recorded by services, and was not checked. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: How many people use test strips when they are offered them depends a lot on the setting. In a paid research study, 77 in 100 young adults who were given ten strips and came back said they had used at least one in the following weeks. At a supervised injection site that offered a check on every visit, about 1 visit in 100 included a check. Across many studies, use ranged from 1 to 80 in 100 people, well below the share who said they were willing. This is what people said or what services recorded; it was not checked.
set.population: People who use drugs offered fentanyl test strips, or attending services that hand them out, in North America: young adults in a paid Rhode Island research pilot (2017); clients of a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016–17); clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); the studies in one scoping review (to March 2023); people using ten British Columbia harm-reduction sites (2019)

evidence_set: Methods › Study Design, 1st paragraph; Methods › Setting; Methods › Variables and Measurement › Exposure › Baseline FTS Use; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

Take-home kits of five strips were handed out with brief peer training at ten British Columbia harm-reduction sites from April to July 2019; no contact or demographic details were collected when kits were handed out and kits not returned were not followed up, so how many kits were used is unknown; the paper reports no number of kits handed out; 336 results sheets were returned.
change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: '62 of the 81 who returned' corrected to '62 of the 81 analysed (83 returned)' (second reader 145); 'did not count the kits it handed out' became 'did not report how many kits it handed out' (the paper reports no number, without saying none was kept; second reader 144), with that point added to the Klaire anchor from the targeted check note (reader 144); the lead and population now include people attending services that hand strips out, since not every client of the US sites was offered strips (second reader 147); the Vickers-Smith anchor's locator adds where the recruitment dates and the 30-day window are given (targeted check note, reader 147); plain text gives 77 in 100. No rating or status changed.

set.statement: In people who inject drugs attending two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (recruited June 2021 to March 2022), recent use of fentanyl test strips was less common a year after the start than at the start, and not clearly different after six months: the adjusted odds of having used strips in the past 30 days were 0.642 times those at the start at 12 months (95% CI 0.447 to 0.923; all 541 people) and 0.557 times (0.364 to 0.853) in the 212 who answered all three surveys, and 0.936 times (0.696 to 1.258) at 6 months, while the share of those 212 who had ever used strips rose from 65 to 80 in 100. The share using strips at each survey is not given in the main text (the supplement, which may give it, was not read), so the size of the fall cannot be given as a number out of 100. The 213 of the 541 who gave no follow-up had less often used strips than the 212 who answered all three surveys (54 against 65 in 100), which could bias the trend, and why use fell was not measured (the authors suggest that a test for fentanyl alone tells people less once fentanyl is expected). Over a few weeks, young adults in a Rhode Island pilot used a median of 3 of the 10 strips they were given (10 of 81 used all ten); in that pilot and in a British Columbia take-home programme, 95 or 96 in 100 said they would use strips again, at the top of the 49 to 96 in 100 that a scoping review relays across studies; these are intentions rather than measures of use. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In the one study that followed people for a year (people who inject drugs at two rural US programmes), fewer had used test strips recently after 12 months than at the start, though more had used them at some point. The study lost many people along the way and did not measure why use fell. In shorter studies about 95 in 100 said they would use strips again, but that is a plan, not a measure.

change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: 'not printed' narrowed to 'not given in the main text', since the unread supplement has descriptive statistics for every wave (second reader 145); the 213 without follow-up are now compared, as in the paper, with the 212 who answered all three surveys, not with everyone followed up (second reader 145); the 49 to 96 in 100 relayed by the scoping review is added from an existing anchor, so that the 95 or 96 in 100 of two programmes is read against the range (second reader 144); plain text gives about 95 in 100. No rating or status changed.

set.statement: In people who use drugs in the United States, mostly recruited at harm-reduction services, and in European drug checking studies relayed by one review, people who use test strips or drug checking differ from people in the same samples who do not, though not in the same ways in every study: in the largest study they more often used fentanyl and injected and already did more to lower their risk, and in a rural cohort they more often used heroin and had seen an overdose, so simple comparisons of the two groups mix any effect of testing with who chooses to test. At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 people who had used strips in the past 30 days and 318 who had not differed in fentanyl use (78 against 59 in 100), injecting (75 against 57 in 100) and ever having been shown how to use strips (76 against 41 in 100); the strip group already reported more of the eight risk-reduction behaviours studied at the start, and its overdose rate was twice as high without adjustment and not clearly different with it (risk ratio 2.06, then 1.20). In rural people who inject drugs (recruited from 2021 and followed for a year), strip use went with having seen an overdose in the past 6 months (adjusted odds ratio 2.444, 95% CI 1.784 to 3.347), heroin use (1.615, 1.107 to 2.357) and being married or living as married (1.521, 1.084 to 2.134), and less with being unhoused (0.679, 0.504 to 0.913), but not clearly with having overdosed oneself (0.981, 0.676 to 1.424) or with fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948 to 1.872). In a small Rhode Island pilot, the 62 who used a strip differed clearly from the 19 who did not only in more often having sold drugs (84 against 58 in 100), and if anything had less often injected (47 against 68 in 100), while among those who used a strip, those whose strip showed fentanyl used heroin weekly far more often (20 of 31 against 3 of 31). In three European studies relayed by a review, clients of drug checking services used ecstasy more often than people in party settings who did not use the services, although in the largest of them people who used the services more often reported using ecstasy less often and less unsafe party behaviour. All characteristics were self-reported, and the two larger studies recruited people at harm-reduction services. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: People who use test strips are not the same as people who don't. In the largest US study they more often used fentanyl and injected, and were already doing more to lower their risk before it began; in another, more of them had seen an overdose. So comparing the two groups cannot tell us what the strips themselves do.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The two larger studies agree that people who use strips differ in risk-related ways (more fentanyl use and injecting in one, more witnessed overdoses and heroin use in the other), though not on the same characteristics; the small Rhode Island comparison (19 people without strips) found no clear difference except dealing, and its injecting figures point the other way (47 against 68 in 100, p = .099).

evidence_set: In three European cross-sectional studies (Belgium, n = 486, 2006; the Netherlands, n = 285, 2002; Austria, the Netherlands and Germany, n = 702, 2002), clients of drug checking services reported more frequent ecstasy use than people in party settings who did not use the services; in the multi-country study, how often people used the services was negatively correlated with how often they used ecstasy and with unsafe party behaviour.
change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: the lead sentence no longer gives every study the same profile: the rural cohort showed no clear link with fentanyl use and everyone in it injected (second reader 145), and in the Rhode Island pilot people who used strips did not use more heroin or see more overdoses and, if anything, injected less (47 against 68 in 100, now in the statement; second reader 145); 'twice as high before allowing for these differences and not clearly different after' became 'without adjustment ... with it', since the overdose model did not adjust for injecting or the earlier behaviours (second reader 147); 'people at the same events' corrected to 'people in party settings', here and in the Maghsoudi anchor (the review does not say they were at the same events; second reader 147, as already corrected by the targeted check in the claim on harms), and the same review's finding that in the largest study more frequent use of the services went with less frequent ecstasy use is added from the anchor; the rural cohort's '(2021 to 2023)' is replaced by its recruitment description, since the end of follow-up is not printed (second reader 145); inconsistency note and plain text aligned. No rating or status changed.

set.statement: At one 25,000-capacity festival in England, the first year with an on-site drug checking service (2016, when chemists analysed 247 samples and staff gave results in 230 consultations, with alerts to on-site agencies), compared with the year before (2015): the evidence is insufficient to say whether the service changed drug-related hospital admissions. The festival's figures, from unpublished police reports, were 19 drug-related admissions among 59 admissions in 2015 and 1 among 50 in 2016; admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49 (editors' calculation), paramedics were said to have treated more people on site rather than sending them to hospital, the partner agencies' data used to judge such outcomes changed between years in the agencies employed and the indicators used and did not always separate drug-related from other incidents, and the author states that the pilot cannot show what part the service played. This was testing by chemists at one festival, with one year before and one after and no comparison festival; it says nothing about kits used at home. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: At one English festival, drug-related hospital admissions fell from 19 in 2015 to 1 in 2016, the first year chemists tested drugs on site. But other admissions rose, paramedics were said to have treated more people on site that year, and the data the agencies kept changed between years, so the study cannot show that the testing caused the fall. The author says the same.

change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: the change of agencies and indicators between years is now worded as the author states it, a general weakness of the partner agencies' data on such outcomes rather than of the admission counts in particular (second reader 145, who found the claim otherwise supported and suitably cautious); plain text aligned. No number, rating or status changed.

set.statement: In people who use drugs given test strips or colour test kits to check their own drugs, handing out kits compared with not handing them out: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it causes harm, for example through false reassurance after a negative result, or reduces harm, and the question is disputed. No study read compared people given kits with people not given them on harm or overdose. What was measured shows few riskier responses: in a British Columbia take-home programme, 6 of 336 survey answers (2 in 100) described using alone or using more or faster after a strip showed fentanyl, in answer to standard questions, and the one study comparing overdoses in people who did and did not use strips found no clear difference after adjustment, in an imprecise estimate (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06). In the Rhode Island pilot, people were told that a negative strip does not rule out fentanyl and to take the same precautions whatever the result. But no primary study read reports what people did after a negative result: the take-home programme asked and did not report the answers, and at the supervised injection site staff recorded only intentions (to use less after 7 of 122 negative checks before use); a scoping review relays one programme in which 10 in 100 women reported a safer change after a negative strip, against 67 in 100 after a positive one. The same review relays people believing that a negative strip means xylazine or that the strength of the line shows how strong the fentanyl is, one person saying a negative result would mean using a little more, a positive result possibly leading people who do not use opioids to think they tolerate fentanyl, and strips giving no information on xylazine and some other drugs and, it says, missing carfentanil, which the laboratory studies read for this page detected on most brands and lots, though only at higher concentrations (see the answer on fentanyl analogues). With take-home strips, people reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples (28 in 100) and 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17 in 100), against 5 of 97 (5 in 100) and 1 of 92 (1 in 100) tested by staff on site, which the authors think more likely reflects how the tests were done than a different supply. Two critiques argue, without data, that frequent positive results without ill effects could breed complacency, that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result, and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe; one of them still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.plain: No study has measured whether handing out test kits causes harm. When people were asked, few said they took more risks after a strip showed fentanyl (about 2 in 100 answers), and one study found no clear difference in overdoses. But the studies read said little about what people did after a strip showed no fentanyl, some people misread strips, strips do not show other drugs such as xylazine, and take-home strips showed fentanyl in stimulants far more often than staff found. Critics worry that a negative result may make people feel safe when they are not; this has not been measured.
set.magnitude: Klaire: riskier responses 6/336 answers (1.8%; Wilson 0.8–3.8%, editors' calculation), 1 using more or faster and 5 using alone; responses to a negative result asked but not reported; take-home strips against on-site checks, crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 points (14.8–30.1), cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), 16.1 (7.1–25.1). Vickers-Smith: nonfatal overdose adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89); composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (0.34–1.38) on 0–15. Karamouzian: intended dose reduction after 7/122 negative checks before use (5.7%). Kutscher (relayed): riskier use in two studies; difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34%; Baltimore programme (103 women), safer change reported by 67% with a positive and 10% with a negative strip. No primary study read reports behaviour after a negative result.

debate.question: Does handing out test strips to people who use drugs reduce harm, or can it cause harm, for example through false reassurance?
debate.evidence_yes: People who found fentanyl often said they then did things thought to lower overdose risk: of 31 young adults in Rhode Island with a positive strip, 45 in 100 said they used smaller amounts, 42 went slower and 39 used with someone else around (Krieger et al., 2018; sc_krieger_2018); at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to use less after 36 in 100 checks before use that showed fentanyl, against 6 in 100 that did not (Karamouzian et al., 2018; sc_karamouzian_2018); a scoping review relays a median of 55 in 100 reporting some safer change across seven studies (Kutscher et al., 2024; sc_kutscher_2024). At a festival where chemists tested drugs, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not as sold handed over drugs for destruction, observed by the service (Measham, 2019; sc_measham_2019). Over four weeks, people who used strips reported more risk-reduction behaviours than people who did not (adjusted difference 0.86 on a 0 to 15 score; for example naloxone nearby, risk ratio 1.10, 1.04 to 1.18), though they already reported more of them at the start (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025; sc_vickers_smith_2025). Riskier responses were rare when asked (6 of 336 answers; Klaire et al., 2022; sc_klaire_2022), and a vending-machine evaluation relayed by the scoping review reports county overdose deaths falling by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%. In the largest of three European studies, people who used drug checking services more often reported using ecstasy less often and less unsafe party behaviour (Maghsoudi et al., 2022; sc_maghsoudi_2022), and a festival evaluation relays reviews that found no rise in drug use, starting use or drug deaths in European countries with drug checking services compared with countries without them (country-level comparisons of services, not of kits; Measham, 2019, citing Brunt, 2012, and others; sc_measham_2019). The critique most cautious about self-testing still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone (McGowan et al., 2018; sc_mcgowan_2018).
debate.evidence_no: No study read shows that handing out strips prevents overdose or death: the only comparison of people who used strips with people who did not found no clear difference in self-reported overdose (adjusted risk ratio 1.20, 0.70 to 2.06; unadjusted 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89) (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025), and the scoping review found only 2 of 91 studies reporting overdose outcomes, neither comparing people who tested with people who did not (Kutscher et al., 2024). Most answers in the take-home programme described no change after a positive result (217 of 336; Klaire et al., 2022), few people intended to throw a drug away after a positive strip at the supervised injection site (11 in 100; Karamouzian et al., 2018), and the review relays people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl. Strips show only whether fentanyl is there, not how much, and as relayed they say nothing about xylazine and other drugs and may miss carfentanil (which the laboratory studies read for this page detected on most brands and lots, though only at higher concentrations); some people misread them (believing a negative means xylazine, or that the strength of the line shows how strong the fentanyl is), a positive result may lead people who do not use opioids to think they tolerate fentanyl (relayed by Kutscher et al., 2024), and with take-home strips people reported fentanyl in stimulant samples about 5 and 16 times as often as staff found on site (editors' calculation, the ratio of the two shares, from Klaire et al., 2022; sc_klaire_2022). Critiques argue that a negative result may falsely reassure (a Health Canada warning about false negatives, cited by McGowan et al., 2018), that frequent positives without ill effects could breed complacency and that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result (McGowan et al., 2018; sc_mcgowan_2018), and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe (Winstock et al., 2001; sc_winstock_2001), which also cites a survey in which 40 in 100 people at clubs said they would take more if pills were thought to have improved. In three European studies, people who used drug checking used ecstasy more often than people in party settings who did not (Maghsoudi et al., 2022; sc_maghsoudi_2022), which may reflect who chooses to test, and a festival evaluation relays critics' concerns, without data, that testing may give an artificial sense of safety and weaken the deterrent effect of drugs' risks by making them seem safer (Measham, 2019; sc_measham_2019).
debate.neither_can_show: Whether handing out strips changes overdose or death: the sources read contain no randomized or well-controlled comparison, and people who use strips differ from those who do not (more fentanyl use and injecting, more earlier risk reduction), so comparisons between them mix testing with who tests. Whether false reassurance happens, and how often: no primary study read reports what people did after a negative result (the supervised injection site recorded only intentions, and a review relays one programme's self-reports), and the harms in the critiques are reasoned, not measured. What people actually took after any result: apart from the festival handovers, the figures are self-reports, intentions or answers to standard questions from people who chose to test. Settings: almost all data come from North American services where fentanyl was common, and the colour-test critique concerns ecstasy pills in Europe around 2000.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the sources read, handing out test strips has not been shown either to cause harm or to prevent overdose. What people say leans towards benefit: after a positive result a minority to a majority report using less or more carefully, and riskier responses were rare when asked; but these are self-reports from people who chose to test and who already did more to lower their risk. The harms the critiques describe are plausible and unmeasured; the largest gap is what people do after a negative result, which no primary study read reports, although one programme asked. The strips' own limits (no amount, missed drugs, misreading, positive readings with take-home strips for stimulants) are facts about the tests, rated in the test-accuracy claims, not evidence of what people then do. The single comparison of overdose is too imprecise to rule out either a benefit or a harm.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized trial or stepped roll-out of strip distribution across sites or areas, with naloxone and the same advice in both arms, recording what people do after positive and after negative results (verified where possible, for example by photographs of strips or laboratory checks of a share of samples), with overdose and death taken from emergency, hospital and death records; and studies that test the same samples at home and in a laboratory, so that how often people meet a false negative in real use is known.

evidence_set: Strips showed fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples tested with take-home strips, used at home, in the street or at supervised sites (27.6%) against 5 of 97 tested on site by trained staff (5.2%), and in 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); different samples were tested, nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, and the study was not powered for stimulants. The authors think how the tests were done a more likely explanation than a differently contaminated supply, citing reports of false positives with stimulants.

Over four weeks, people who used strips at baseline had an adjusted composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (95% CI 0.34–1.38) on a 0–15 scale, and reported more naloxone nearby (RR 1.10, 1.04–1.18), testing the strength of drugs before use (1.41, 1.24–1.61), asking someone to check on them (1.26, 1.10–1.45) throwing out bad or unexpected drugs (1.50, 1.12–2.01) and watching someone use the same drugs first (1.19, 1.04–1.36), but less use by routes other than injection (0.86, 0.79–0.94); self-reported nonfatal overdose: adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89).

evidence_add.extracted: Relayed, without data of the author's own: critics' concerns that testing at best gives an artificial impression of safety (citing Winstock et al., 2001), that results may be inadequate, that dealers may use services for quality control, that services focus on contaminants rather than risky behaviours, and that testing may reduce the deterrent value and raise the appeal of drugs by making them seem safer; and, on the other side, that two decades of Dutch testing and alerts had no perverse effect on drug use or drug-related deaths, and that there is no evidence that drug prevalence, initiation or mortality rose in European countries with drug safety testing compared with those without (citing Benschop et al., 2002; Brunt, 2012; Hungerbuehler et al., 2011). These are country-level comparisons of services, not of kits.
